0700: Social login can hand an attacker someone else's account. And the fix is one check. Your app reads the email from the login token, finds a matching account, and signs the user in. But some identity providers let people use an email they never verified. So an attacker signs up with your customer's email, and walks straight into their account. The check: only link accounts when the provider confirms the email is verified. And make the existing user prove it is them first.
0900: Why does a European bank make you prove it is you twice? It is the law, and the hard part is not where you think. Under strong customer authentication, most online payments in the EU and the UK need two of three things. Something you know, like a PIN. Something you have, like your phone. Something you are, like a fingerprint. There are exemptions for low value and low risk payments. For engineers, the hard part is not the second factor. It is handling exemptions and failed challenges without losing the customer.
1300: One line in a cloud policy can give away your whole account. Action star. Resource star. It usually starts as a quick fix to get a deploy working, and it never gets removed. Now any leaked key for that role can read your data, delete your backups, and create new admins. The fix has three steps. One. Give every service its own role. Two. Grant only the actions it uses. Three. Find permissions nobody has used in ninety days, and remove them.
1500: The most useful security meeting takes fifteen minutes and four questions. What are we building? What can go wrong? What are we going to do about it? Did we do a good job? It is Adam Shostack's four question framework, and it works because product teams can answer it without security jargon. Ask it at design time, not after launch, and write the answers down. Senior security engineers do not hold every answer. They make sure the questions get asked.
1700: Your AI assistant just read an email that told it to forward your invoices. And it did. That is indirect prompt injection. Any text the model reads, an email, a web page, a document, can carry instructions, and the model cannot reliably tell yours from an attacker's. So do not rely on it to. Three guardrails. Give the assistant only the tools it needs. Treat its output as untrusted. And require a human click before it sends, pays or deletes anything.
1900: Your CEO asks: are we secure? The wrong answer is yes. A better one: here are our three biggest risks, what each would cost, and what we are doing about them. What would you say?
